A contemporary is a person who lives — or lived — during the same period of time as another person.

That's the heart of it. The word is entirely about shared time. Not shared place, not shared profession, not shared ideas — just time.
A Simple Example to Lock It In

Imagine two great painters: Leonardo da Vinci and Michelangelo. They both lived and worked in Italy during the same era — the late 1400s and early 1500s. Neither one came 200 years before or after the other.

This means:

Michelangelo was a contemporary of Leonardo da Vinci.

Or you can flip it:

They were contemporaries.

Both sentences mean exactly the same thing: these two people existed at the same point in history.
It Works for the Present, Too

The word doesn't only apply to historical figures. You can use it for living people right now.

"Elon Musk and Mark Zuckerberg are contemporaries."

Both are alive and active in the world today. Same era. That makes them contemporaries.

You can even use it personally:

"She is a contemporary of mine."

This simply means: she and I belong to the same generation or time period — perhaps we went to school in the same years, or built our careers around the same decade.
Being Contemporaries Does NOT Mean They Knew Each Other

This is a very important distinction that trips up many learners.

Two people can be contemporaries and never have met, spoken, or even heard of each other. The word makes no claim about any relationship between the people. It only tells you they shared the same slice of history.

For example, a farmer in China in the year 1600 and Shakespeare in England in the year 1600 were contemporaries — they lived at the same time — but clearly had no connection whatsoever.
The Time Period Can Be Broad or Narrow

There is some natural flexibility in how precisely you define "the same period."

  • In a historical discussion, "contemporaries" might mean people from the same century or era.
  • In a professional discussion, it might mean people from the same generation — perhaps within 10–20 years of each other.
  • In a personal discussion, it often means people who grew up or studied or worked at roughly the same time.

Context usually makes the meaning clear. The word stretches or tightens depending on the scale of the conversation.

You will encounter the plural — contemporaries — extremely often, perhaps more than the singular. It's used when talking about a group of people from the same era.

"Newton was ahead of his contemporaries."

This means: compared to all the other thinkers who lived during Newton's time, Newton was exceptionally advanced.

"She outlived most of her contemporaries."

This means: most of the people who were born and lived around the same time as she did have already died, but she is still alive.

When someone says "his contemporaries," they mean the people of his time — not people of your time reading about him today. The word always anchors itself to a specific person's era as the reference point.

So if you read: "Darwin's contemporaries were skeptical of his theory," it means the scientists and thinkers who were alive when Darwin was alive were skeptical — not scientists today.

What it meansA person who lives/lived during the same time period as another
What it's aboutTime, and time alone
What it does NOT implyAny relationship, friendship, or awareness between the people
Common plural use"her contemporaries," "his contemporaries" = the people of that same era

Once you understand that this word is purely a time marker for people, you will never misuse or misread it again. Whenever you see it, simply ask yourself: "Who else was alive or active at the same point in history?" — and that is exactly what the word is pointing to.
